title: AI Agents
tagline: What happens when a language model gets hands.
description: From a model that can only talk to a system that acts: tools, loops, plans, memory, coordination — and the guardrails that keep an acting system honest. The running case study is a real production agent.

intro.hook: A model that only answers is a tool. A model that can act, observe and try again is something else.
body: Ask a language model a question and you get text. Give that same model the ability to run a search, call an API, read the result and decide what to do next, and the character of the thing changes: it can now pursue a goal across many steps, recover from its own mistakes, and do work rather than describe it.

That loop — think, act, observe, repeat — is the entire idea. Everything else is engineering: how to give it tools safely, how to keep it on task, how to stop it confidently doing the wrong thing at scale.
The failure modes are as instructive as the successes, and considerably less discussed.

why.title: From answering to doing
why.text: Multi-step work with real tools is the difference between a chatbot and something that finishes tasks.

why.title: The loop is the architecture
why.text: Think, act, observe. Almost every agent framework is a variation on those three steps.

why.title: Safety is a design problem
why.text: Permissions, verification and blast radius are not add-ons. They are what makes an agent usable at all.

intro.closer: The hard part was never getting an agent to act. It was getting it to stop when it should.

concepts.title: What makes it an agent
concepts.summary: Model + tools + a loop + state. The model proposes; the harness executes; the result feeds back.

cards.h: A chatbot answers. An agent acts.
cards.md:
Ask a chatbot to 'check whether the backup ran' and it can only tell you *how you might check*. An **agent** runs the command, reads the output, and answers from evidence.

The difference is not a smarter model — it is **architecture**. An agent is a loop wrapped around a model:

1. The model reads the goal and the state so far.
2. It proposes an **action** (call a tool, run a query, send a message).
3. The harness (the code wrapping the model) **executes** the action and appends the result.
4. Repeat until the model decides it is done.

Every serious agent — coding assistants, research agents, the personal agent this course uses as its case study — is some version of that loop. The model never touches the world directly; it emits *intentions*, and a harness with permissions decides what actually runs.

Strip any agent to its frame and you find the same four parts:

- **The model** — proposes the next action. Swappable; the frame outlives any given model.
- **Tools** — the verbs: read a file, query a database, send an email. Each is a typed function the model can request.
- **The loop** — feeds tool results back so the next proposal is informed by what just happened.
- **State** — the conversation, tool outputs, and whatever memory persists across turns.

A useful mental test: *where does new information enter?* In a chatbot, only from the user. In an agent, mostly from **tool results** — the world talks back. That feedback channel is what makes agents powerful, and it is also where most of their failure modes live: a wrong tool result, trusted blindly, corrupts everything downstream.

cards.h: Case study: one loop, one hundred verbs
cards.md:
The case-study agent (a personal quant assistant) is a plain Python loop — deliberately **not** a framework. One process reads a Telegram message, builds a prompt with relevant memory, and lets the model call from ~100+ registered tools: market-data queries, email, calendar, portfolio lookups, a web dashboard.

Why hand-rolled? **Control over the loop is control over safety.** Every tool call passes through one gate that knows each tool's risk level (read-only vs write vs money-adjacent), rate limits, and whether it needs operator confirmation.

The designers' rule of thumb, learned the hard way: *the part that must not fail should contain no intelligence at all.* Reminders, backups, and alerts run on deterministic schedules — the model composes and reasons, but arithmetic decides when the alarm fires.

questions.prompt: What most fundamentally separates an agent from a chatbot?
options: A larger, smarter language model
A loop in which the model's proposed actions are executed and the results fed back
Access to more training data
A personality and long-term goals
feedback: Model quality helps everything, but a bigger model with no tools and no loop is still just a better talker.
Right. Act → observe → act again. The feedback loop through the real world is the defining structure.
Training data shapes what the model knows, not whether it can act on the world.
Persona is cosmetic. Plenty of agents have no personality at all — schedulers, pipelines, CI bots.

questions.prompt: In a well-designed agent, who actually executes a dangerous action like deleting a file?
options: The model, directly — that's what makes it an agent
The harness, after checking permissions and possibly requiring confirmation
The user, always, by hand
Nobody — agents are read-only by definition
feedback: The model only ever emits a *request*. If the model could act directly, no permission system could ever be trusted.
Right. The model proposes; the harness disposes. The gate between intention and execution is where safety lives.
Requiring a human for every action gives up the point of an agent. The design question is *which* actions need a human.
Agents write, send, and trade in production every day — behind gates, not behind a blanket ban.

questions.prompt: Why did the case-study agent move reminders OUT of the model's hands onto a deterministic scheduler?
options: The model was too slow to fire alarms on time
Deterministic code is cheaper to run than model calls
Every model-dependent hop is a place a critical action can silently fail
Language models cannot read clocks
feedback: Latency wasn't the issue — a reminder fired two seconds late is fine. A reminder silently *lost* is not.
True but not the reason. The cost of a model call is trivial next to the cost of a missed deadline.
Right. A reminder once vanished across three model-dependent hops. The lesson became a design rule: the part that must not fail contains no intelligence.
Models handle time fine. The problem is reliability of the whole chain, not clock-reading.

concepts.title: Tool use
concepts.summary: Tools are typed functions the model can request. Schemas tell it how; risk levels decide what happens next.

cards.h: How a model calls a function
cards.md:
A tool is described to the model as a **schema**: a name, a purpose sentence, and typed parameters.

```json
{"name": "etf_query",
 "description": "Run a read-only SQL query against the ETF warehouse",
 "parameters": {"sql": {"type": "string"}}}
```

When the model wants the tool, it emits a structured call — `etf_query(sql="SELECT ...")` — instead of prose. The harness validates the arguments against the schema, runs the real function, and appends the result to the conversation.

Two things follow. First, **the description is an interface contract**: the model chooses tools by reading it, so a vague description produces wrong tool choices. Second, **validation is the harness's job** — the model will sometimes emit malformed or even dangerous arguments, and the schema layer is the first place to catch that.

Reading a price is not the same risk as sending an email, which is not the same as moving money. Mature agents encode this as **per-tool risk levels**.

The case-study agent tags every tool: `read-only` tools run freely; `write-local` tools (file writes, DB (database) inserts) run with logging; `write-network` tools (email, messages) pass policy checks — recipient allowlists, rate limits, body caps; anything financial is **recommend-only**: the agent produces an order sheet, a human executes it.

The pattern generalizes: **capability should be granted per-verb, not per-agent.** An agent with a hundred tools where five are dangerous needs five gates — not blanket trust, not blanket paranoia. And the gate lives in the harness, where the model cannot talk its way past it.

cards.h: The tool result is testimony, not truth
cards.md:
A subtle failure class: the tool ran fine, but its *output* is wrong or stale — an API (Application Programming Interface) served another fund's holdings, a cache went sour, a scraper read a redesigned page.

Agents that treat every tool result as ground truth inherit every upstream data bug. The case-study agent learned this repeatedly: a data vendor once served fund X's holdings under fund Y's name, and only a *cross-write hash guard* (does this payload exactly match another fund's book?) caught it.

Defenses worth copying: **provenance** on every stored result (which source, when), **plausibility gates** at the write door (a $437B claim for a fund reporting $1.77B does not get written), and **verify-before-overwrite** when two sources disagree. The loop makes the model powerful; the guards make the loop trustworthy.

questions.prompt: Why does the quality of a tool's description matter so much?
options: It is displayed to end users in the UI
The model selects and uses tools by reading their descriptions — it is the interface contract
Longer descriptions make tool calls run faster
It is legally required documentation
feedback: Users rarely see tool schemas. The reader that matters is the model itself.
Right. A vague description produces wrong tool choices and malformed arguments. Writing tool descriptions is prompt engineering.
Description length has no effect on execution speed.
Nothing legal about it — it's an engineering interface.

questions.prompt: An agent has 100 tools; 5 can move money or send external messages. The sound design is:
options: Require human confirmation for all 100 tools
Trust the agent fully — it was tested
Per-tool risk levels: free reads, logged writes, gated or human-executed high-risk verbs
Remove the 5 dangerous tools entirely
feedback: Blanket confirmation trains the human to click 'yes' without reading — which is worse than fewer, meaningful gates.
Testing shows presence of capability, not absence of failure. One bad tool call can be unrecoverable.
Right. Capability per verb: the gate matches the blast radius, and it lives in the harness where the model can't argue with it.
Sometimes right! But if the capability is needed, the answer is gating — e.g. recommend-only order sheets a human executes.

questions.prompt: A tool call succeeds (no error) and returns data. What can still be wrong?
options: Nothing — a successful call means correct data
The data itself: stale, mislabeled, or wrong at the source
Only formatting issues
Success codes are random, so everything
feedback: A 200 OK means the pipe worked, not that the water is clean. Upstream data bugs arrive with success codes.
Right. A vendor once served one fund's holdings under another fund's name — clean call, poisoned payload. Provenance and plausibility gates exist for exactly this.
Formatting is the easy case — schemas catch it. The hard case is well-formed wrong data.
Success codes are meaningful; the point is they certify transport, not truth.

resources.label: Schick et al. — Toolformer (arXiv)
resources.note: The research moment tool-calling became mainstream: models teaching themselves when to call APIs.

resources.label: Model Context Protocol
resources.note: The emerging open standard for exposing tools to any agent — schemas, servers, permissions.

concepts.title: The reasoning loop
concepts.summary: ReAct: interleave thinking and acting, observation by observation — and know when to stop.

cards.md:
The pattern that unlocked modern agents is embarrassingly simple. Instead of asking a model to answer in one shot, you let it alternate:

**Thought:** 'The question needs the fund's expense ratio (its annual fee) — I should query the warehouse.'
**Action:** `etf_query(...)`
**Observation:** `0.19%`
**Thought:** 'Now I can compare it against the category median...'

This is **ReAct** (Reason + Act, Yao et al. 2022). Its power comes from *grounding*: each reasoning step conditions on real observations rather than on the model's guesses. The model doesn't have to know the expense ratio — it has to know **how to find it**, which is a much easier and much more reliable skill.

The practical consequence: an agent's competence is bounded less by what its model memorized and more by what its tools can reach.

A loop needs a reason to stop. Agents fail at both ends:

- **Stopping too early** — answering from memory when one more tool call would have grounded the claim.
- **Not stopping** — re-trying a failing action forever, or wandering through irrelevant tool calls, burning budget.

Production agents bound the loop three ways: **step budgets** (max tool calls per turn), **cost budgets** (tokens/dollars), and **progress checks** (is the latest observation new information, or are we circling?). The case-study agent adds per-task-type budgets — a quick lookup gets a small budget; a research task gets a big one.

Design intuition: budgets are not just cost control. A model that knows it has three calls left *prioritizes differently* — scarcity forces the plan to surface.

cards.h: Failure inside the loop is information
cards.md:
In a one-shot system, an error is the end. In a loop, an error is an **observation** — often the most informative one.

A tool returns 'no such table'? The agent lists tables and corrects the name. A rate limit? Wait and retry, or switch sources. The file doesn't exist? Search for where it moved.

This is why agents feel qualitatively different from chatbots in practice: they **debug their own attempts**. The skill of using error text as a steering signal — read the message, form a hypothesis, adjust — is most of what separates a capable agent from a flailing one.

But note the precondition: errors must *reach* the loop honestly. A harness that swallows failures and returns something error-shaped-but-vague ('task failed') robs the model of exactly the signal it needs. Honest plumbing is an intelligence multiplier.

questions.prompt: Why does the ReAct pattern reduce hallucination compared with one-shot answering?
options: Interleaved reasoning steps make the model more careful by nature
Each reasoning step can condition on real observations from tools instead of the model's guesses
It uses more tokens, and more tokens mean more accuracy
It doesn't — ReAct is about speed
feedback: The care isn't in the model's nature — it's in the structure: claims get checked against the world as it goes.
Right. The model needs to know how to FIND facts, not to have memorized them. Retrieval-grounded steps beat recalled 'facts'.
Token count alone buys nothing. Grounding is what changes: guesses get replaced by observations.
ReAct is usually slower than one-shot. The win is reliability, not latency.

questions.prompt: An agent keeps calling the same failing API with the same arguments, 40 times. What design element is missing?
options: A bigger model
Progress checks and budgets that bound the loop
More tools to choose from
A friendlier error message from the API
feedback: Even strong models loop when nothing in the harness measures progress. This is a loop-design bug, not an IQ bug.
Right. Step budgets, cost budgets, and 'is this observation new information?' checks are the brakes a loop needs.
More options don't help an agent that isn't noticing it's stuck.
Clearer errors help the first retry. The 40th identical retry is a missing-brakes problem.

questions.prompt: Why is a harness that silently swallows tool errors ('task failed, moving on') harmful to agent quality?
options: It slows down execution
Error text is the steering signal the model uses to debug its next attempt — hiding it removes the signal
It makes logs larger
It isn't harmful; errors just upset the model
feedback: Speed is unaffected — quality is what dies.
Right. 'No such table: etf_metric' tells the model exactly what to fix. 'Task failed' teaches it nothing. Honest plumbing is an intelligence multiplier.
Log size is irrelevant here.
Models don't get upset — they get uninformed, which is worse.

resources.label: Yao et al. — ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting (arXiv)
resources.note: The loop that defines modern agents, in its original form. Skim §2 for the pattern.

concepts.title: Planning and decomposition
concepts.summary: Big tasks need structure: plan-then-execute, interleaved planning, and the art of right-sized steps.

cards.md:
**Plan-then-execute:** the agent writes a full plan up front ('1. fetch the data, 2. clean it, 3. run the comparison, 4. write the report'), then works through it. Predictable, auditable, easy to show a human for approval — but brittle when step 2 reveals that the plan was wrong.

**Interleaved planning** (the ReAct default): plan only as far as the next action; re-plan after every observation. Adaptive — but can lose the thread on long tasks and wander.

Production systems blend them: a **coarse plan** for shape and approval, **fine-grained interleaving** inside each step. The case-study agent's build pipeline does exactly this — an approved objective and staged milestones on the outside, free tool-by-tool adaptation inside each stage.

Rule of thumb: plan at the level where surprises are rare; interleave at the level where they are common.

cards.h: Decomposition is where quality is won
cards.md:
Ask an agent to 'audit the database' and you get shallow coverage of everything. Ask it to run **twelve named checks** — duplicate identifiers, shared prospectus URLs, cloned holdings, impossible inception dates... — and you get depth on each.

Decomposition converts one vague goal into many verifiable sub-goals. Each sub-goal gets its own success criterion, which means failures localize: check #7 failed, the rest stand.

This is also the honest-reporting trick: a decomposed task can report **partial success truthfully** ('11 of 12 checks clean; holdings-clone found 2 pairs'). A monolithic task can only report vibes. When you see an agent produce a crisp, itemized result, the quality was usually won at decomposition time, not at answer time.

Every plan is implicitly a spend: tool calls, tokens, minutes. Mature agents make it explicit.

The case-study system routes tasks by **type**, and each type carries a budget: a market-data lookup gets a handful of calls on a fast local model; a nightly research study may get hours on a large one. When a task starts blowing through its budget, that itself is a signal — either the task was misclassified, or it is stuck.

A subtler point: **budget shapes behavior**. Agents given unlimited steps procrastinate — verifying trivia, re-checking done work. Agents with tight budgets skip verification they should have done. Somewhere between is a budget that forces prioritization without forcing corner-cutting; finding it per task-type is real tuning work, not a default you can guess.

questions.prompt: When is plan-then-execute the wrong choice?
options: When the task needs human approval before starting
When early steps are likely to reveal information that invalidates later steps
When the task has more than three steps
It is never wrong — planning always helps
feedback: Approval is exactly where up-front plans shine — a human can read the plan before anything runs.
Right. If step 2's observation routinely rewrites steps 3-6, plan at coarse grain and interleave the detail.
Step count alone doesn't decide it — predictability of the terrain does.
A rigid plan over surprising terrain is actively worse than adaptive stepping.

questions.prompt: Why does decomposing 'audit the database' into 12 named checks improve honesty, not just quality?
options: Smaller prompts are cheaper
Each check has its own pass/fail, so the agent can report partial results truthfully instead of vibes
It prevents the model from seeing the whole database
Twelve is a lucky number in QA
feedback: Cheaper, sometimes — but that's economics, not honesty.
Right. '11 of 12 clean, holdings-clone found 2 pairs' is checkable. 'The database looks fine' is not.
Scope control isn't the point; verifiable sub-goals are.
A joke option — the number of steps follows from the task's structure and the agent's own decomposition, not superstition.

questions.prompt: An agent with an unlimited step budget tends to:
options: Perform identically to a budgeted one, just cheaper
Fail immediately
Procrastinate — re-verify done work and polish trivia, because nothing forces prioritization
Always find better answers
feedback: Behavior actually changes with budget — scarcity is a forcing function.
No — it fails slowly, which is more expensive.
Right. Budgets aren't just cost control; a model that knows it has three calls left plans differently.
More steps past the useful point add cost and stale-context risk, not quality.

concepts.title: Memory
concepts.summary: Context is rented, memory is owned: what to persist, how to retrieve it, and why write-time beats read-time.

cards.h: The context window is not memory
cards.md:
A model's context window is **working memory**: whatever fits, it can use; the moment the conversation ends (or overflows), it is gone. Agents that 'remember' do so with an external store the harness consults.

The standard split:

- **Short-term:** the current conversation + recent tool results. Free, automatic, evaporates.
- **Long-term:** facts worth keeping — preferences, decisions, verdicts, past failures. Must be *deliberately written* and *deliberately retrieved*.

The deliberate part is the design problem. Store everything and retrieval drowns in noise; store too little and the agent re-asks what it was told last week. The working answer in most production agents: store **conclusions, not transcripts** — the verdict with its evidence pointer, not the 40-message conversation that produced it.

cards.h: Retrieval: the memory is only as good as the lookup
cards.md:
A memory nobody can find is a memory that doesn't exist. The two dominant retrieval styles:

- **Keyword / full-text search:** exact and predictable — great when your vocabulary is stable ('TC-1c', 'Convex Core').
- **Embedding similarity:** finds semantically related notes with different wording — and also finds seductive near-matches that are actually irrelevant.

The case-study agent audited its own 'memory misses' and found something instructive: the search engine was fine — the misses were **wrong-tool choices** (the model didn't search at all) and **content gaps** (the fact was never written down). They kept plain FTS (full-text search) and rejected a fancier hybrid, because without a relevance floor, semantic search mostly added noise.

Moral: before upgrading the search algorithm, measure *why* recall fails. It is usually the write side, not the read side.

cards.h: Write-time discipline: cite or it didn't happen
cards.md:
The nastiest memory failure is not forgetting — it is **remembering something false**. An agent that writes a wrong 'fact' to memory will confidently repeat it for months.

The case-study system was burned exactly once: the agent wrote a fabricated note into its knowledge vault. The fix was structural, not hopeful: **every durable note must cite a checkable source** — a file, a commit, an email id — and an automatic audit rejects notes whose numbers don't appear in the cited artifact. A note the audit cannot open is treated as indistinguishable from a fabricated one.

General principle: memory quality is enforced at **write time**, when the evidence is at hand — not at read time, when the evidence is long gone and the note just looks authoritative.

questions.prompt: Why do production agents store 'conclusions, not transcripts' in long-term memory?
options: Transcripts are legally sensitive
Retrieval quality: a concise verdict with an evidence pointer is findable and reusable; 40 raw messages are noise
Storage is expensive
Models are not allowed to read old conversations
feedback: Sensitivity varies, but that's a different policy question.
Right. The failure mode of store-everything is drowned retrieval. Memory is a curation problem before it is a storage problem.
Text is cheap. Attention — at retrieval time — is what's scarce.
They can; it's just rarely the best use of context.

questions.prompt: The case-study team audited memory 'misses' and found the search engine was fine. What were the real causes?
options: Hardware failures corrupting the index
Wrong-tool choices (never searched) and content gaps (never written) — write-side and routing problems
The embeddings were too small
Users asking unanswerable questions
feedback: The index was healthy — the audit checked.
Right. Their fix was steering (when to search) and write discipline (what to store) — and they deliberately REJECTED a fancier hybrid search that would have added noise.
They weren't using embeddings — plain full-text search, kept on purpose.
The questions were answerable; the facts just weren't stored or weren't looked for.

questions.prompt: Why enforce memory quality at WRITE time (citations, audits) instead of read time?
options: Writing happens less often, so it's cheaper to check there
At write time the evidence is at hand and checkable; at read time a false note just looks authoritative
Read-time checks would slow down conversations
It's arbitrary — either works
feedback: Frequency helps, but that's not the core reason.
Right. A note that cites a commit can be audited the moment it's written. Months later, a confident-sounding note is nearly impossible to falsify in-flight.
Latency is a minor factor next to falsifiability.
They are not symmetric: evidence decays. Write-time is when the receipt exists.

concepts.title: Grounding and hallucination
concepts.summary: An acting system must not invent facts. Grounding ties every claim to a tool result — mechanically, not aspirationally.

cards.h: Hallucination gets expensive when systems act
cards.md:
In a chatbot, a made-up number is embarrassing. In an agent, it can become an **action**: an email sent to the wrong person with wrong figures, an order sheet with an invented price, a 'confirmed' backup that never ran.

The root cause is unchanged — a language model is a plausibility machine, and plausible-but-false is its natural failure mode. What changes with agents is the **remedy**: because the agent has tools, every factual claim *can in principle be traced to a tool result*. Grounding is the discipline of making that tracing real.

Weak grounding: 'the model usually checks.' Strong grounding: the harness **verifies mechanically** that the numbers in the answer actually appeared in the evidence — and blocks the reply when they didn't.

cards.h: Case study: a guard that reads every reply
cards.md:
The case-study agent runs an anti-fabrication guard on financial responses. The idea is simple and brutal: build a **grounding pool** — every number that appeared in this turn's tool results (plus numbers the user themselves supplied) — then scan the model's reply for numeric claims. A number with no source in the pool blocks the reply.

What production taught them:

- **False positives are the real war.** CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) colors (`#666`), years, tickers-that-look-like-numbers — each needed an explicit carve-out, found by replaying blocked turns.
- **The guard needs an escalation path**, not just a wall: a blocked turn can retry with a hint ('ground the numbers or drop them').
- Verdicts like 'this subtotal is wrong' were sometimes the *guard being right* against a confidently wrong model — the audit trail settles the argument.

cards.h: Verify claims the way an auditor would
cards.md:
Grounding numbers is the mechanical layer. Above it sits a broader honesty discipline for agent claims:

- **'It works' requires a run.** An agent claiming success on a task it never executed is the same failure as a fabricated number. The case-study system added a sentinel: a turn that claims completion with zero tool calls gets flagged.
- **'It's fixed' requires the failing case to pass.** Re-run the exact reproduction, not a vibe-check.
- **'The data says X' requires the query to be shown.** Answers that cite their own evidence can be re-checked later; answers that don't are folklore in a week.

The pattern across all three: convert claims into **checkable artifacts**. An agent whose statements come with receipts can be trusted with bigger verbs; one whose statements don't, cannot — no matter how smart its model is.

questions.prompt: Why is hallucination strictly more dangerous in an agent than in a chatbot?
options: Agents hallucinate more often
A fabricated fact can become an executed action — an email, an order, a config change
Agent hallucinations are harder to detect by reading
It isn't — same risk, same stakes
feedback: Rates are similar for the same model; the *consequences* differ.
Right. Action converts a wrong belief into a wrong state of the world. That's why grounding must be mechanical, not aspirational.
Detection is comparable; blast radius is not.
The stakes change the moment claims drive actions.

questions.prompt: The case-study fabrication guard blocks replies containing numbers absent from the grounding pool. What was the hardest ongoing engineering problem?
options: The guard was too slow
False positives — legitimate numbers (CSS colors, years) misread as ungrounded claims
The model learned to evade the guard
Nobody could read the guard's code
feedback: A regex pass over a reply is microseconds.
Right. Guards live or die on FP rate: every false block erodes trust in the guard. They replayed blocked turns to find and carve out each FP class.
The model doesn't see the guard to game it — it's harness-side.
It's a small, auditable module — that's rather the point.

questions.prompt: An agent reports 'done ✅' on a task, and the log shows zero tool calls that turn. What is the correct system response?
options: Trust it — the model probably remembered the task was easy
Flag it: a completion claim with no actions is the action-shaped version of a fabricated number
Ask the model if it is sure
Lower the temperature
feedback: Tasks don't complete themselves. Zero actions + a success claim is the signature of a confabulated completion.
Right. The case-study system calls this the silent-failure gate: no false '✅ complete' on zero-tool turns.
The model that fabricated the claim will happily confirm it.
Temperature tweaks don't fix structural honesty gaps.

questions.prompt: In one or two sentences: why is a successful tool call's output 'testimony, not truth'?

grading.model_answer: A success code certifies the transport, not the content — the data can still be stale, mislabeled, or wrong at the source, so it must be treated as a claim to check (provenance, plausibility) rather than ground truth.

rubric.expects: confuses 'the call worked' with 'the data is right'
rubric.feedback: The key split is transport vs content: a 200 OK certifies the pipe, not the water.

rubric.expects: asserts tools are reliable so output can be trusted
rubric.feedback: Upstream sources DO serve wrong data with clean success codes — the case study's vendor served one fund's holdings under another fund's name.
This one isn't about the model hallucinating — it's about the TOOL's data being wrong while the call succeeds.

questions.feedback_correct: Exactly — success codes certify transport; content needs its own checks.

resources.note: Training-side honesty pressure — complementary to the harness-side guards this concept covers.

concepts.title: Multi-agent systems
concepts.summary: Fan out for breadth, verify adversarially, synthesize once — and pay the coordination tax knowingly.

cards.md:
Three honest reasons to split work across agents:

1. **Breadth** — ten reviewers each reading one subsystem cover a codebase no single context window can hold.
2. **Independence** — five ideators who cannot see each other's answers produce genuinely different options; one model asked five times produces variations on its first idea.
3. **Adversarial checking** — a verifier prompted to *refute* a finding catches what the finder's confirmation bias missed.

And one dishonest reason, worth naming: *it sounds impressive.* Multi-agent systems pay a real *coordination tax* — results must be merged, conflicts resolved, context re-explained to every worker. A single competent agent with good tools beats a committee of confused ones. The case-study shop's rule: fan out when the task exceeds one context or one perspective — not before.

The dominant production pattern is a hub: an **orchestrator** decomposes the task, dispatches **workers** with self-contained briefs, and synthesizes their reports.

The load-bearing detail is the **brief**. A worker arrives with empty context; everything it needs — the goal, the constraints, where to look, what shape to return — must be in its instructions. Vague briefs produce confident essays about the wrong thing. The case-study shop writes worker briefs with a return-schema ('respond with JSON (JavaScript Object Notation): {finding, file, line, severity}'), which forces structure and makes synthesis mechanical.

Peer-to-peer agent swarms exist in research, but audits of production systems keep finding the same thing: hierarchies win, because synthesis needs one place where conflicting reports get resolved — and one throat to choke when the answer is wrong.

The most reliable use of multiple agents is not parallel *production* — it is parallel *verification*.

The pattern, from the case-study shop's review fleet: finders sweep a codebase for bugs; each candidate finding then goes to independent **skeptics** prompted to refute it ('assume this is a false positive; prove it'). A finding survives only if the refuters fail. This kills the plausible-but-wrong findings that a single reviewer waves through — at roughly 3× the cost, which is cheap next to one bad finding shipped.

Variants: give each verifier a different *lens* (correctness, security, does-it-reproduce) rather than three identical skeptics; or score proposals with a judge panel and synthesize from the winner. The shared principle: **independence at generation time, adversarial pressure at acceptance time.**

questions.prompt: Which task genuinely benefits from multiple agents rather than one good agent?
options: Renaming a variable across one file
Auditing a codebase far larger than any single context window, then merging findings
Answering a factual question
Formatting a document
feedback: One agent, one minute. Fan-out here is pure coordination tax.
Right. Breadth beyond one context is the cleanest justification for fan-out — with a synthesis step at the end.
A lookup needs a tool, not a committee.
Deterministic scripts beat agents entirely for this.

questions.prompt: Why do production multi-agent systems put a return-schema in every worker's brief?
options: It reduces token costs
Structured returns make synthesis mechanical and force the worker to answer the actual question
Schemas prevent workers from using tools
It's a legacy convention from REST APIs
feedback: Sometimes marginally — but that's not why.
Right. Free-prose reports from five workers are five essays to reconcile. Five JSON objects merge in a loop.
Schemas shape the OUTPUT, not the tool access.
Convergent, but the reason is synthesis, not tradition.

questions.prompt: In the finder/skeptic verification pattern, why are the skeptics prompted to REFUTE findings rather than to 'double-check' them?
options: Refutation prompts are shorter
A 'double-check' inherits the finder's framing and confirms it; an adversarial stance actively hunts the failure mode
Skeptics are cheaper models
It makes the logs more dramatic
feedback: Length is irrelevant.
Right. 'Verify this' produces agreement; 'assume it's false and prove it' produces scrutiny. The asymmetry is the entire value.
Skeptics are often the SAME model — the prompt stance is what differs.
The drama is a side effect.

resources.note: The reference framework paper for conversational multi-agent patterns.

resources.label: Anthropic — How we built our multi-agent research system
resources.note: Production notes on orchestrator-worker research agents — briefs, parallelism, and what broke.

concepts.title: Evaluating agents
concepts.summary: Did it actually work? Task-level success, regression pins, shadow modes — and the benchmark trap.

cards.h: Evaluate the task, not the vibes
cards.md:
Agent evaluation has one honest question: **did the task end in the state the user wanted?** Not 'was the answer fluent' — did the test pass, the email send, the number match the warehouse.

That makes agent evals harder *and* easier than chatbot evals. Harder: you need an environment where actions have checkable effects (a repo, a database, a sandbox). Easier: success is often binary and mechanical — `SWE-bench` (a software-engineering benchmark) counts a fix as solved only if the repo's own tests pass afterward.

The trap is **proxy drift**: measuring steps-taken, tokens-used, or self-reported confidence because outcome checking is expensive. Every proxy invites the agent (and its developers) to optimize the proxy. If the outcome can be checked mechanically, check the outcome.

Production agents improve by accumulating **pins** — tiny tests that encode a specific past failure so it can never silently return.

The case-study repo is full of them, each with a story: the reminder that vanished across model-dependent hops (pin: capture path has zero LLM hops), the snooze that instantly re-fired (pin: the next tick after a snooze is silent), the guard that blocked a CSS color as a fabricated number (pin: `#666` passes).

This is the agent-era version of regression testing, with a twist: many pins test the *harness around* the model rather than the model itself, because the harness is where reliability actually lives. A model upgrade can shift behavior overnight; the pins are what tell you which lessons survived the upgrade.

cards.h: Shadow mode: evaluate in production, act later
cards.md:
The safest way to evaluate a risky new capability: run it in **shadow** — it sees real inputs and produces real decisions, but its output is logged instead of executed.

The case-study shop shadows almost everything before arming it: a data-quality guard runs for weeks in log-only mode (how many false positives *would* it have blocked?), a self-healing retry logs the fix it *would* have applied, a fleet watchdog runs 48 hours of dry-run before its alerts go live — armed only after a clean record.

Shadow mode resolves the evaluation dilemma for systems whose mistakes are costly: offline benchmarks are unrealistic, live trial-by-fire is reckless. The pattern costs patience and a little logging code, and it converts 'we think it's safe' into a measured false-positive rate you can defend.

questions.prompt: SWE-bench counts a coding-agent run as successful only when the repository's own tests pass on the patched code. Why is this a better metric than expert ratings of the patch?
options: Experts are too expensive
It is a mechanical outcome check — the state of the world, not an opinion about the artifact
Tests are always right
Ratings are illegal for benchmarks
feedback: Cost matters but isn't the principle.
Right. Outcome-grounded evals resist charm: a beautiful-looking patch that breaks the suite scores zero.
Tests can be wrong — but they're checkable and fixed in advance, which ratings are not.
Not a real constraint — rating-based evaluation is standard practice; its genuine problems are subjectivity and cost, not legality.

questions.prompt: What is a regression 'pin' in an agent codebase?
options: A bookmark to important code
A small test encoding a specific past failure so it can never silently recur
A version-locked dependency
A high-priority ticket
feedback: Close in spirit, but pins EXECUTE.
Right. Each pin is a frozen lesson — and because many pin the harness, they also tell you which lessons survive a model swap.
That's dependency pinning — same word, different tool.
Tickets describe; pins enforce.

questions.prompt: Why run a new alerting system in dry-run/shadow mode for 48 hours before arming it?
options: To warm up caches
To measure its would-fire behavior (especially false positives) on real inputs before its mistakes can cost anything
Because systemd requires it
To give the model time to learn
feedback: Caches are irrelevant here.
Right. Shadow mode converts 'we think it's safe' into a measured record — the case-study watchdog armed only after 0 false alerts in the window.
No such requirement.
Nothing is training during shadow — it's the HUMANS learning the system's behavior.

resources.label: Jimenez et al. — SWE-bench (arXiv)
resources.note: The outcome-grounded coding benchmark: real issues, real repos, the repo's own tests as judge.

concepts.title: Guardrails and containment
concepts.summary: Permissions, confirmation gates, sandboxes, and the principle of least privilege — safety as architecture.

cards.md:
The foundational rule of agent safety predates agents by decades: **grant the minimum capability the task needs.**

Applied to agents it becomes concrete: the model gets tools, not shells; each tool gets the narrowest scope that works (a `read_file` restricted to the workspace directory, not the filesystem); secrets stay in the harness (the model composes an email — it never sees the SMTP (email-sending protocol) password); and money-adjacent actions are **recommend-only** by construction.

The payoff shows up on the worst day: when the model is confused, deceived by a malicious input, or just wrong, the damage is bounded by the permission map — not by the model's judgment. Safety you can compute from config beats safety you have to trust from behavior.

Confirmation prompts fail in a predictable way: put one on *everything* and the human learns to click yes — the gate becomes theater.

Production discipline: **gate rarely, gate hard, and never let the gate be bypassed upstream.** The case-study agent reserves confirmation for genuinely irreversible verbs (external emails to new recipients, destructive file ops), keeps reads free, and — after losing a reminder to a confirmation that never got answered — moved *capture* paths to zero-gate deterministic code entirely.

Second, subtler rule: a gate must **fail closed and honestly**. If the audit log isn't writable, the risky verb refuses to run — a gate that silently passes when its bookkeeping is broken is worse than no gate, because it launders unaudited actions as audited ones.

Agents increasingly install other people's capabilities — community 'skills', plugins, MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers. Each one is **someone else's instructions and code running inside your agent**, and the supply-chain risk is real: a malicious skill can exfiltrate whatever the agent can see.

The case-study approach, worth copying wholesale: **pin, scan, jail.** Pin the exact version (a git SHA, a commit fingerprint — upstream can't silently swap the code later); scan it before install (and read the findings — their scanner's repo-level CRITICAL turned out to be false positives on image bytes, while the actual payload was clean; both facts mattered); run it in a credential-free container with no network unless the skill's function requires it.

And the meta-rule: treat *content* a skill fetches as data, never as instructions — the prompt-injection boundary is a guardrail too.

questions.prompt: Why is 'the model never sees the SMTP password' a stronger guarantee than 'the model is instructed not to reveal it'?
options: Instructions cost tokens
Architecture cannot be talked out of: what the model never had, it cannot leak, no matter how it is manipulated
Passwords confuse models
It isn't stronger — both work equally well
feedback: Trivially true, irrelevant.
Right. Behavioral rules bend under clever prompting; capability boundaries don't. Compute safety from config, don't trust it from behavior.
Models handle secrets fine — that's the problem.
A determined prompt injection defeats instructions; it cannot conjure a secret the harness never exposed.

questions.prompt: Putting a confirmation prompt on every single agent action leads to:
options: Maximum safety
Habituated approval — the human rubber-stamps everything, and the gates that matter drown in the ones that don't
Faster workflows
Better audit logs
feedback: It optimizes the FEELING of safety while destroying the mechanism.
Right. Gate rarely and hard. The case-study shop even removed gates from capture paths after one unanswered confirmation ate a critical reminder.
Obviously slower — and less safe, which is the surprise.
Logs improve with logging, not with prompts.

questions.prompt: Before installing a third-party skill, the case-study shop pins the git SHA, scans the tree, and runs it in a credential-free jail. What threat does the PIN specifically counter?
options: Prompt injection in the skill's output
Upstream silently replacing the vetted code with something malicious after you audited it
Excessive token usage
License violations
feedback: That's what the data-not-instructions boundary is for.
Right. A vet is only as durable as the immutability of what you vetted. The pin freezes the audited artifact; a drift-watch flags when upstream moves.
Budgets handle that.
A license check is separate diligence.

resources.label: Simon Willison — Prompt injection series
resources.note: The clearest ongoing writing on why 'content as instructions' is the agent-era vulnerability class.

concepts.title: Failure modes and honesty
concepts.summary: Loops, confabulated success, silent death — and why honest failure is a feature you must build.

cards.md:
Agent failures cluster into a few recurring shapes:

- **The loop** — same action, same failure, forever. Missing progress checks.
- **The wander** — plausible-looking tool calls drifting away from the goal. Missing plan discipline.
- **The confabulated success** — 'done ✅' with nothing done. The worst one, because it *reports* as health.
- **The poisoned observation** — a wrong tool result trusted and propagated.
- **The silent death** — the process stops and nothing notices.

Notice what's common: four of the five are **detectable by the harness** without any intelligence — step counters, completion sentinels, plausibility gates, watchdogs. Reliability engineering for agents is mostly classical systems engineering wearing a new hat.

The scariest state for an autonomous system is *quiet*. Healthy-quiet and dead-quiet look identical from the outside — unless you engineer the difference.

The case-study stack, bottom to top: the agent pushes a **heartbeat** to an external service every 10 minutes (if the pings stop, something off-box notices); a second, independent probe on another machine watches from inside the LAN (Local Area Network); watchdog crons (scheduled jobs) check data freshness and service health with debounced state machines; and an unacknowledged critical alert **escalates** rather than expiring — an unanswered reminder is treated as a failed one.

The design principle: **silence is only allowed to mean health if something would provably scream otherwise.** Every quiet channel needs a dead-man behind it — belt, suspenders, and a second pair of suspenders on another machine.

The deepest lesson from running agents in production is cultural, not technical: **an agent's value is capped by how much you can trust its reports.**

An agent that says 'I ran 46 checks; 3 failed, here are the failing cases' is useful even when it fails. An agent that rounds every outcome up to '✅ done!' is dangerous even when it succeeds — because you can no longer tell the difference. That's why the machinery in this course keeps recurring on one theme: grounding guards, completion sentinels, cite-on-write memory, shadow modes, pins. They are all **honesty infrastructure**.

The compounding effect is real: every honest failure report tightens the loop (the failure gets a pin, the pin prevents the recurrence); every dishonest success report poisons it. Capability gets the demos. Honesty gets the production deployment.

questions.prompt: Why is 'confabulated success' ranked the worst failure mode?
options: It costs the most tokens
It reports as health — the system's own signals say everything is fine while the task silently didn't happen
It crashes the process
It only happens with small models
feedback: Cost is trivial next to trust.
Right. A crash pages someone; a false '✅' teaches you to stop checking. It corrupts the only channel you monitor.
Exactly the opposite — everything keeps running, which is the trap.
Every model does it under the wrong incentives; the fix is harness sentinels, not model size.

questions.prompt: What does the dead-man's-switch pattern guarantee that ordinary error alerting cannot?
options: Errors get prettier formatting
Detection of SILENT death: if the system stops entirely, the absence of its heartbeat is itself the alarm — raised off-box
Fewer false alarms
Faster reboots
feedback: Cosmetics don't matter to a dead process.
Right. A dead system cannot send its own error alert. Only an external observer expecting a heartbeat can notice nothing arriving.
It adds an alarm class; false-positive tuning is separate (debounce).
Detection first — recovery is a different layer.

questions.prompt: 'Honesty is a capability' — what is the engineering content of that slogan?
options: Models should be fine-tuned to be polite
Trustworthy self-reporting is BUILT — sentinels, grounding guards, cited memory, shadow modes — and it, not raw skill, gates what you can safely delegate
Honest agents are slower, and that's fine
It's a marketing phrase without engineering content
feedback: Politeness is orthogonal to truthfulness.
Right. Every honest failure tightens the loop (failure → pin → never again); every false success poisons it. The infrastructure that enforces receipts is what makes delegation rational.
The overhead is small, and the alternative caps the agent's usable autonomy regardless of speed.
It compresses a real design doctrine — most of this course's machinery is honesty infrastructure.

resources.label: Shinn et al. — Reflexion (arXiv)
resources.note: Agents that learn from their own failure traces — the research face of 'honest failure tightens the loop'.

resources.label: Anthropic — Building effective agents (closing guidance)
resources.note: Ends where this course does: start simple, add autonomy only as trust is earned.

preface.hook: A calculator waits for you. An agent goes off and does things — which is a much bigger difference than it sounds.
body: A normal program does exactly what it was told, once, and stops. You ask a calculator for eight times seven and it answers. It has no plan and nothing to decide.
An agent is given a goal instead of an instruction. Book me a table somewhere nice on Friday. Now it has to work out steps, look things up, notice when something failed, and try again differently.

That is built by looping. It thinks about what to do, takes one action, looks at what happened, and repeats. The looping is the entire trick — a single answer becomes a sequence of moves that respond to what it finds.

Which introduces a problem that did not exist before: it can be wrong in the middle and carry on confidently. A calculator giving one wrong answer is one wrong answer. An agent misreading step two can spend twenty more steps building on the mistake.

So most of the real work is not making them capable. It is making them checkable — proving what they actually did, limiting what they are allowed to touch, and having them stop and ask rather than guess when the goal is unclear.

aha.title: The loop is the whole idea
aha.text: Take away 'look at the result and decide the next move' and you have an ordinary program again. Everything impressive and everything alarming about agents comes from that one addition.

aha.title: Errors compound
aha.text: A small misunderstanding early gets built upon, so by step fifteen the work can be confidently and completely wrong. This is why good agent design checks progress rather than only checking the final answer.

aha.title: Permissions matter more than cleverness
aha.text: The interesting question is rarely 'can it do this'. It is 'what can it reach, and what happens if it is wrong'. An agent that can only read is a very different proposition from one that can send and delete.

preface.closer: Give it a goal instead of an instruction, and everything changes.
